---
title: "Loading a structured data file"
subtitle: "Open a CSV file. Examine what R received."
description: "Learn how rows, columns, missing values, and text encodings affect a CSV file in R."
categories: [source data loading, CSV, data quality]
---

Before a community team's weekly meeting, a coordinator receives one CSV file
containing feedback from email, web forms, and live chat. The group plans to
examine low ratings. First, the coordinator must find what the five records
contain and whether loading changed their structure.

A file can open without an error even when a column is missing, an accent is
damaged, or an identifier changes format. A reader can also mistake a blank
rating for a score unless they know its meaning. We will examine the file's
raw lines, then find the one low rating.

We will run the checks again on a second export. That export contains a repeated
identifier, an impossible rating, and a row with too many fields.

::: {.callout-note}
The author created these fictional feedback records for teaching. They do not
describe real people or customers.
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- explain how a structured data file organizes information.
- load a CSV file into R.
- examine rows, columns, and data types.
- find missing values.
- examine the parse problems, duplicate keys, and out-of-range values in a
  flawed file.
- select records that meet a stated condition.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## What makes a file structured?

What does each part of the file represent? A
**structured data file** follows a consistent arrangement. In a CSV file:

- each **row** usually represents one record.
- each **column** represents one kind of information.
- commas separate one column from the next.

CSV stands for **comma-separated values**. The first line often contains the
column names. Quotation marks enclose text containing a comma so the comma
remains part of the text. A quoted field can also contain a line
break, so one physical line does not always equal one record. A quotation mark
inside a quoted field usually appears twice.

Before asking R to make a table, the coordinator reads the file as plain lines.
`read_lines()` from readr returns one text value for each physical line. The output shows the first three stored lines.

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)

file_path <- "data/customer_feedback.csv"
file_lines <- read_lines(file_path)

head(file_lines, 3)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(file_lines), 6L),
  identical(
    file_lines[1],
    "feedback_id,submitted_at,channel,rating,comment"
  ),
  str_detect(file_lines[2], fixed('"Delivery was quick, thank you!"'))
)
```

The file has six lines: one header and five records. Quotation marks keep the
first comment's comma inside one field rather than separating columns.
This line count works because the teaching
file has no quoted line breaks.

## Load the CSV into R

The line count and header match expectations. The next step organizes the
records. The readr function `read_csv()` converts the file into a **tibble**, a
table that prints its size and each column's type. By default, readr interprets
text as UTF-8, an encoding for characters from many languages.
It therefore uses UTF-8 to read the accented text.

```{r}
feedback <- read_csv(
  file = file_path,
  na = "",
  col_types = cols(
    feedback_id = col_character(),
    submitted_at = col_character(),
    channel = col_character(),
    rating = col_integer(),
    comment = col_character()
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  feedback,
  col.names = c("Feedback ID", "Submitted", "Channel", "Rating", "Comment"),
  caption = "Customer feedback loaded from the CSV file",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  inherits(feedback, "tbl_df"),
  identical(nrow(feedback), 5L),
  identical(ncol(feedback), 5L),
  identical(
    names(feedback),
    c("feedback_id", "submitted_at", "channel", "rating", "comment")
  ),
  identical(feedback$feedback_id, as.character(1001:1005)),
  identical(
    feedback$comment[2],
    "The café listing was easy to find."
  )
)
```

All five records appear in five columns. The comma in the first comment stayed
inside the comment, and the accented letters in `café` display correctly. The
final comment, `"Muy útil y fácil de usar"`, is Spanish for "Very useful and
easy to use."

The teaching file's data dictionary defines a blank rating as missing.
`na = ""` applies that rule while loading. A real project should use the
missing-value rules supplied by its data provider. Do not treat the literal text `"NA"`, zero, and a blank field as equivalent
without such evidence.

Those checks show that loading preserved the visible layout. We still
need to examine how R interpreted each column.

### Why choose the column types?

The `col_types = cols(...)` setting tells readr which **data type** to use for
each column. A data type records whether values should behave as text, whole
numbers, dates, or another kind of information.

- identification numbers are text because they identify records.
- dates begin as text so we can convert them deliberately.
- ratings are whole numbers.
- channels and comments are text.

Treating an ID as text protects leading zeros. For example, the label `"0012"`
should remain different from `"12"` when that difference exists in the source.

We can ask R to report the type it used for every column. `map_chr()` from
purrr applies the same check to each column and returns a character vector.
The shorthand `\(column)` means "for each column, run the small calculation that follows."

```{r}
column_types <- map_chr(
  feedback,
  \(column) class(column)[1]
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    column = names(column_types),
    type = unname(column_types)
  ),
  col.names = c("Column", "Type used by R"),
  caption = "The type assigned to each column",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    unname(column_types),
    c("character", "character", "character", "integer", "character")
  )
)
```

R reports `character` for text and `integer` for whole numbers. Here,
`character` is R's name for text. A value may contain an entire comment.
Choosing these types deliberately prevents R from converting record labels to
quantities.

## Convert the date column

The submission dates are text. The dplyr function `mutate()` changes a
column while keeping the rest of the table. Here `as.Date()` converts the text
to R's date type. The coordinator can then sort and compare calendar dates.

```{r}
feedback <- feedback |>
  mutate(
    submitted_at = as.Date(
      submitted_at,
      format = "%Y-%m-%d"
    )
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  feedback |>
    select(feedback_id, submitted_at, channel),
  col.names = c("Feedback ID", "Submitted", "Channel"),
  caption = "Submission dates after conversion",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  inherits(feedback$submitted_at, "Date"),
  identical(
    range(feedback$submitted_at),
    as.Date(c("2026-08-21", "2026-08-25"))
  )
)
```

The format `%Y-%m-%d` means four-digit year, two-digit month, and two-digit day.
Writing it explicitly records the order expected in this file rather than
requiring the reader to guess.

## Find missing information

After examining rows, columns, and types, the coordinator finds absent
values. R uses `NA` to represent a **missing value**. The CSV
contains one blank rating, which `read_csv()` changed to `NA`. `map_int()`
returns one whole-number count for each column.

```{r}
missing_counts <- map_int(
  feedback,
  \(column) sum(is.na(column))
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    column = names(missing_counts),
    missing_values = unname(missing_counts)
  ),
  col.names = c("Column", "Missing values"),
  caption = "Missing values in each column",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(unname(missing_counts), c(0L, 0L, 0L, 1L, 0L)),
  is.na(feedback$rating[3])
)
```

The rating column has one missing value. A blank means only that this file
records no rating. It differs from a rating of zero.
Do not replace the blank without evidence about its meaning.

## Select a record that needs attention

Only now does the coordinator select feedback with a rating of two or lower.
`filter()` from dplyr keeps rows that meet a condition, and `select()` keeps the
columns needed for the meeting. The expression `!is.na(rating)` excludes the unknown rating from the comparison
rather than treating it as high or low.

```{r}
low_ratings <- feedback |>
  filter(!is.na(rating), rating <= 2) |>
  select(feedback_id, rating, comment)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  low_ratings,
  col.names = c("Feedback ID", "Rating", "Comment"),
  caption = "Feedback with a rating of two or lower",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(nrow(low_ratings), 1L),
  identical(low_ratings$feedback_id, "1004"),
  identical(low_ratings$rating, 2L)
)
```

One record meets the condition: feedback `1004`, which says that the parcel
arrived late. The missing rating remains separate because the file does not
tell us how that person would have scored the experience.

## When the next file is not clean

The first file was well formed. The next example represents another export
from the same web form. The lesson defines the text directly rather than
reading a saved file, so each line remains visible.

The six records contain six features to examine. These include a repeated
`feedback_id`, a rating typed as a word, and a row with an extra field.
Another rating exceeds the documented range of one to five.
The file also contains a blank rating and a quoted comment across two physical
lines.

```{r}
messy_text <- paste(
  "feedback_id,submitted_at,channel,rating,comment",
  "1006,2026-08-26,email,4,\"Arrived on time\"",
  "1006,2026-08-26,email,4,\"Second row with the same ID\"",
  "1007,2026-08-27,chat,five,\"Rating typed as a word\"",
  "1008,2026-08-27,web,3,\"Extra field\",unexpected",
  "1009,2026-08-28,web,9,\"Rating outside the documented range\"",
  "1010,2026-08-28,email,,\"Comment that runs\non to a second line\"",
  sep = "\n"
)

messy_lines <- read_lines(I(messy_text))
messy_feedback <- suppressWarnings(
  read_csv(
    I(messy_text),
    na = "",
    col_types = cols(
      feedback_id = col_character(),
      submitted_at = col_character(),
      channel = col_character(),
      rating = col_integer(),
      comment = col_character()
    )
  )
)
messy_raw <- suppressWarnings(
  read_csv(
    I(messy_text),
    na = character(),
    col_types = cols(
      feedback_id = col_character(),
      submitted_at = col_character(),
      channel = col_character(),
      rating = col_character(),
      comment = col_character()
    )
  )
)

tibble(
  measure = c("Physical lines", "Records read"),
  count = c(length(messy_lines), nrow(messy_feedback))
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(messy_lines), 8L),
  identical(nrow(messy_feedback), 6L),
  identical(nrow(messy_raw), 6L),
  identical(
    names(messy_feedback),
    names(feedback)
  )
)
```

Eight physical lines produced six records because one quoted comment contains
a line break. The earlier line-count check worked only because that file had
no quoted line breaks.

`suppressWarnings()` appears because this page treats warnings as errors.
Suppressing the warning does not discard the evidence. readr keeps a structured
report of everything it could not parse.

### Read the parse problems

```{r}
parse_problems <- problems(messy_feedback) |>
  transmute(
    row,
    record_number = row - 1L,
    feedback_id = messy_raw$feedback_id[record_number],
    col,
    expected,
    actual
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  parse_problems,
  col.names = c(
    "File row",
    "Record",
    "Feedback ID",
    "Column",
    "Expected",
    "Found"
  ),
  caption = "What readr could not parse",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  inherits(parse_problems, "tbl_df"),
  identical(nrow(parse_problems), 2L),
  identical(
    parse_problems$expected,
    c("an integer", "5 columns")
  ),
  identical(
    parse_problems$actual,
    c("five", "6 columns")
  ),
  identical(parse_problems$feedback_id, c("1007", "1008"))
)
```

readr counts the header line. Reported row 4 is therefore the third record,
whose rating is `five`. The parser changed that value to `NA`.
For the extra-field row, the parser added the unexpected text to the comment.

A parse problem does not always produce a missing value. A missing value does
not always indicate a parse problem.

The same checks apply in other languages. In pandas, `dtype` and `na_values`
declare column types and missing-value rules. Arrow can use an explicit schema.
Keep the parser's problem report with those declarations.
An unreported parser guess creates a risk in any language.

### Examine what a parser cannot establish

Successful parsing confirms the expected structure. It does not establish that
identifiers are unique or ratings are possible. The data dictionary supplies
those rules. Each rule can become a check that reports a failure.

```{r}
documented_rating_range <- 1:5
parse_failure_ids <- parse_problems |>
  filter(expected == "an integer") |>
  pull(feedback_id)
extra_field_ids <- parse_problems |>
  filter(expected == "5 columns") |>
  pull(feedback_id)

row_report <- messy_feedback |>
  mutate(
    record_number = row_number(),
    raw_rating = messy_raw$rating,
    duplicate_id = feedback_id %in%
      feedback_id[duplicated(feedback_id)],
    parse_failed = feedback_id %in% parse_failure_ids,
    declared_missing = raw_rating == "",
    rating_out_of_range = !is.na(rating) &
      !(rating %in% documented_rating_range),
    extra_field = feedback_id %in% extra_field_ids,
    status = case_when(
      duplicate_id ~ "quarantine: repeated feedback_id",
      parse_failed ~ "quarantine: rating failed integer parsing",
      rating_out_of_range ~ "quarantine: rating outside 1 to 5",
      extra_field ~ "quarantine: unexpected sixth field",
      declared_missing ~ "keep: rating recorded as missing",
      TRUE ~ "keep"
    )
  )

status_counts <- row_report |>
  count(status, name = "records")

quarantined <- row_report |>
  filter(str_starts(status, "quarantine"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  row_report |>
    select(record_number, feedback_id, raw_rating, rating, status),
  col.names = c(
    "Record",
    "Feedback ID",
    "Raw rating",
    "Parsed rating",
    "Decision"
  ),
  caption = "All records with reasons for inclusion or exclusion",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(sum(status_counts$records), 6L),
  identical(nrow(quarantined), 5L),
  identical(
    quarantined$feedback_id,
    c("1006", "1006", "1007", "1008", "1009")
  ),
  identical(
    sum(row_report$parse_failed),
    1L
  ),
  identical(
    sum(row_report$declared_missing),
    1L
  ),
  identical(
    n_distinct(messy_feedback$feedback_id),
    5L
  )
)
```

The report excludes five of six records for different reasons. Two share an
ID. The source must explain the duplicate before either can identify record
`1006`. The raw value `five` failed integer parsing and differs from an ordinary
missing rating. One row has an unexpected sixth field. Another has a rating of
nine, which exceeds the dictionary's maximum.

The remaining record has a blank rating. A blank that the dictionary defines as
missing is not a parse error.

The report classifies all six input records and omits none without explanation.
Filtering to usable rows alone would report one record. That output would omit
the evidence of a duplicate ID in the source.

## Questions to ask about any structured file

The five-row check is complete, but structural checks cannot answer every
question about the feedback. Before an analysis of any structured file, ask:

1. What does one row represent?
2. What does each column mean?
3. Which encoding does the file use?
4. How are missing values recorded?
5. Are dates and identification numbers stored correctly?
6. Who created the file, and what information did they exclude?

A tidy table cannot tell you whether the collection process was fair or
complete. These rows represent only the feedback that reached the recorded
channels and was included in this file. The file's origin, exclusions, and
limits belong alongside the technical checks.

## What to remember

- A structured file uses a consistent arrangement of rows and columns.
- Quotation marks protect text that contains a separator such as a comma.
- Quoted line breaks make physical lines and records different counts.
- Choose important column types rather than relying on guesses.
- Read the parser's problem report instead of only its output table.
- Uniqueness and value ranges come from the data dictionary, not the parser.
- Examine missing values before filtering or summarizing.
- Opening a file successfully does not complete the required checks.

At the meeting, the coordinator can report five records, one missing rating,
and one recorded rating of two. The second file contains six records.
One is usable, and five remain excluded for stated reasons.
The blank remains missing, and the file's coverage remains uncertain.

Report the recorded values and missing values. State which questions the file
cannot answer.
